title: Pommes frites
subtitle: Proper twice-fried French chips
excerpt: Thick-cut potato sticks fried twice: once at low temperature to cook them through, then at high temperature to make them golden and crisp. The classic French accompaniment to steak and most grilled meat.
sourceNotes: The twice-frying method for chips is a well-established French technique described in Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903, multiple public-domain editions) and in Auguste Escoffier's Ma Cuisine (1934). The method of first frying at a low temperature to cook through, then finishing at high temperature for crispness, is the classical French frite technique.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The first fry can be done up to 2 hours ahead. Drain the chips on kitchen paper and hold at room temperature, then do the second fry just before serving.

content.text: Pommes frites are the classic French chips: thick-cut, cooked twice, and served hot enough to burn your fingers. The two-stage method is what separates them from a single-fry chip: the first stage cooks the potato through at a low temperature, the second stage at high heat creates the crisp golden exterior.

items.prepNote: floury variety, peeled, cut into 1 cm square sticks

content.text: Rinse {{potato}} of cut potatoes in cold water until the water runs clear. Dry very thoroughly on a clean cloth or kitchen paper. Any surface water will cause the oil to spit.

Heat the oil in a large, deep, heavy pan to 140°C. Working in batches that leave plenty of room, lower the chips into the oil and cook for 6 to 8 minutes until cooked through but with almost no colour. Lift out with a slotted spoon and drain on kitchen paper. Repeat with the remaining chips. Leave to cool to room temperature.

Raise the oil to 190°C. Lower the par-fried chips back in, again in batches, and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until deep golden and crisp all over. The oil will bubble vigorously at first, then settle. Lift out, drain on fresh kitchen paper, and season immediately with sea salt flakes.
Serve at once. Pommes frites do not hold well.

items.cause: Oil was not hot enough for the second fry, or chips were still wet
items.fix: Use a thermometer and wait for the oil to fully recover to 190°C between batches. Dry the raw chips thoroughly before the first fry.

items.symptom: Chips are dark outside but raw in the middle
items.cause: Skipped the first fry, or first-fry oil was too hot
items.fix: The first fry at 140°C is what cooks the inside. Do not rush it.

items.cause: Chips were wet when they went in
items.fix: Rinse, then dry thoroughly. Lower chips in gently; never drop them from a height.

items.cause: Oil temperature dropped too far when chips were added
items.fix: Fry in smaller batches so the temperature stays stable.

content.text: The pomme frite is inseparable from French bistro cooking: it comes alongside steak, moules, and simple grilled fish as a matter of course. The twice-fried method is standard in professional French kitchens, where the first fry (the blanching stage) can be done during service prep and the second fry done to order. Belgium also has an equally strong claim on the chip: fried in beef fat, sold in paper cones at street stalls, eaten with mayonnaise. Both are right.
